MADAME, THE AEROPLANE IS ADVANCED

To take flight, one must wear a special garment of thick Suède, trimmed with fur, and a helmet that rises like the helm of the Middle Ages. With as much assurance as she mounts in her automobile, the woman of today may fly in a last-cry limousine.
By Betty Thornley
Original Drawings by Paul Iribe

To prepare for rescue is secured; clac... the cabin is closed… Then, with lowered eyes for one last glance at the poor humanity that remains below, and the aeroplane glides, boum… boum… all along the great grassed field… faster, faster, with that particular sensation of a rush of clouds arriving in your face and wires of iron stretched vibrating wildly. Faster, faster. If one were to enter the wind, faster... faster...

Can words ever render this extraordinary sensation, unlike anything else, even for someone who has lived the most adventurous life? This strange feeling experienced at the instant when, for the first time, the wheels detach—the aeroplane does not lift with a bound as an automobile starts: it caresses for a few instants the field from which it rises, jumping over ruts and then, suddenly, it lifts, and you feel in the depths of your heart triumphant. It is not fever. It is like an elevation of the heart, like a constriction of the throat, like a rustling in your ears, and you exclaim: "I knew it, I knew it, this is the sensation that I have always awaited, I was born for it, I never wish to live without it again!"

And while you utter these words, you rise ten meters, twenty meters, thirty meters. The hangar diminishes like the tail of an express train receding in the perspective of a prairie. Houp… It is a shock, a mountain of air that strikes you, as a wave would enfold you on the beach at Dinard. One has never seen a wave with the force to elevate one above the water. It is the climate of the atmosphere which is the cause, varying according to the altitude from which one rolls like…

Imagine a field of golden sunlight or a verdant meadow, or the shimmering surface of water. For the first time you experience the peculiar effect of an air pocket, one feels as if an elevator were plummeting from a house fifty stories high; the second time, oh, you pay far less attention; the third time, your brain adapts in a manner involuntary and almost as though it accepted the air pocket in the same way one was taught, years ago, to allow oneself to be carried by the breaking wave; and after that you think no more of air pockets, for you will encounter them no longer once you have left the lower layers of the atmosphere and abandoned these troubled regions.

IN THE OCEAN OF AIR

Now lean over the edge of your nacelle, look down...down… into this strange, colourless ocean which you had never contemplated and knew only because you breathed within it. Perhaps you are one of those persons who could not put their head out of a bedroom window if that window were higher than a fifth story; perhaps you can recall the horrible sensation you experienced the first time you ascended the Tour Eiffel many years ago, and gazed into the void through its metallic framework.

You now imagine that you are not merely gazing into the void but are actually above it, and your feet do not touch the ground; for it is true, you are incomparably further from the earth than you have ever been before; you have no point of comparison, no walls, no precipices, no mountains, nothing save this extraordinary and invisible mattress of air.

Below you, at leagues’ distance, appear patches of colour: houses, probably, taut threads which are roads, a brilliant mirror: the sea. But you perceive them simply as one perceives… when she descends from her aeroplane, the trousers of her costume form an ordinary, correct overcoat. 

There are no birds in the sky today; there are not even clouds except for a few delicate laceworks of mist at six thousand meters or less. Nothing can indicate to you the altitude at which you find yourself save the sensation of your own heart, but you know that you are at an immense height because you no longer distinguish…

The railways run upon the earth, because the green of the meadows and the yellow of the harvests mingle for you into a homogeneous shade; a few glimmers sparkle towards the south over lakes and ponds that one glimpses through the trees; further on, toward the north, you distinguish the small pointed line of a lighthouse and then, gradually, you forget all these things, all these trivial details without importance which melt into the eternal face of the globe as far as you can contemplate it, and the droning of the machine that lifts you, to the buzzing of the wind and to this singing fever of the wires within which pass like agitations of wings...

Formerly, you crept; now you fly; you are a soul of steel, a Valkyrie of 150 horses with twelve-meter wings; you can travel 200 kilometers an hour and you prove it.

Life today knows the trembling and expansion that come to it from the addition of a fifth direction. Before the war, you could go north, south, east, west; you could go as far as the sea, you could go as far as the mountains, you could travel to Berlin or return to Paris, but you could not do so at the same time even if you had agreed to climb the summit of Mont Blanc and freeze your ears in August. There are being organised aerodromes near New York, and the student whose university lies 200 kilometers distant could, whenever he pleases, attend the theatre. Before these European results (and one could multiply them infinitely) we must conclude that America is completely surpassed, even in the West. It is not that this country lacks aerostatic science, oh no; from a commercial point of view, America possesses the largest aeroplane factories which exist in the world. The United States has 8,000 patents from Curtiss factories. American pilots hold the height records; America organised the first aerial circuit around the world and offered considerable prizes. America has held its place at all the most important conferences that have been held on the subject of aviation.

“Fins Voiliers de l’Air” – “Wings like Sailing Ships.” The engineers of the Curtiss factory intend shortly to produce an aeroplane absolutely perfect, which will rapidly ascend to the height where winds no longer exist and will speed along at 200 kilometres per hour, or more, and these brilliant swiftnesses of the air will permit New York financiers to travel to Chicago for an important conference in less than three hours if the wind is favourable; as the air will be artificially condensed and heated in the cabin where our financier sits, he will suffer no inconvenience. For the return journey, his skilled pilot will know how to find the height where the winds blow in the right direction, and it will not cost him a sou more for that.

During the entire time, on both the outward and return journeys, our financier may dictate or smoke, or read, or converse, or even sleep in oblivion of all this universe which forms the association. It is a century where joys and sorrows mingle.

The Society of Air Transport in the United States is certainly one of the largest societies imaginable; however, it must be recognized that it has not yet been acknowledged by great aerial organizations, and that far too many Americans are led to believe that flying is not only the privilege of a few select individuals but also of people particularly skilled and trained. Now, it is not only Santos-Dumont who can fly, nor merely Lieutenant Reid or all the Guynemer or all the Nungesser – it is also John Morgan and Cortlandt Morgan his wife, and Madeleine Morgan his daughter, and her two little darlings.

Yes, there is something altered in the world of Aviation; there are truly no difficulties in flying; there is no question of money to go breathe the true pure air for a few hours, but only to address a competent engineer, a trained pilot, and make one’s request to the Aero Club of America in order to obtain an aviator's license.

Here is a blouse from Piguet in painted grey silk gauze. France permits relatively warm fabrics for travel because the temperature fluctuations there are abrupt and frequent. One sees here and there charming alpaca dresses. They are mostly of a great simplicity, often of redingote form like that of Jenny on the left. The redingote is skillfully cut in narrow sections and soutacheed in grey.

A reminder of the season’s infatuation with Egyptian ornamentation is suggested by the Egyptian embroidery plaque in old-blue, yellow, and dark red concealed beneath the belt. This model has a typical gilet in white organdi, particularly practical for travel. The long waistline that Jenny always favors continues to make the skirt the most important part of the costume.

This typical gown, by Lanvin, features ballooning ruffles of silver lace, evoking the dances of the eighteenth century while remaining the most modern dress, destined for the latest mode. A sage green taffetas is restrained by matching cords and may be worn with two skirts – one to be tied about the waist, the other to fall freely. It truly is perfect for all occasions.

The vova’s three coats from Jenny combine serge and foulard—either plain or patterned—marking quite often a tendency to bring back volume on the front; indeed, some afternoon or evening dresses of this season feature it. A satin coat of black has the back straight and the front of considerable amplitude, drawn in under a low satin belt fastened with an Egyptian ornament in turquoise. Other pieces from the collection are embellished with grey and rust, colour combinations favoured by Jenny.

THE ROBE-COAT

The robe de Beer reproduced on page 9 to the left shows a clever combination of dress and coat, suggested by Chéruit last season, which is particularly indicated for the woman who travels with little baggage. We are no longer certain of receiving our trunks quickly upon arrival, and for travelling one often prefers to take only hand luggage. A coat or a serge overcoat covering entirely the garment beneath is invaluable in such circumstances.

These coats may be worn with a checked foulard in soft, muted shades of red and blue. Here is one of the charming emanations of summer: tulle of a cloudy grey, citron crepe, and roses so large that only a slender young woman can wear them with grace. This coat, one of the lighter coats of this season, allows its wearer to take tea or dine in intimacy. The dress is embroidered with pearls in a motif recalling the old tapestries of Paris.

The beach at Biarritz is of a dazzling whiteness at all times of the year; it is animated by the presence of the most elegant society one could find; there are three distinct seasons: an English, a French and a Spanish.

VOGUE
IN AUTOMOBILE from the CÔTE D'ARGENT to the CÔTE D’AZUR
FRANCE

L comes to launch an appeal to motorists of all countries; she invites them to come and explore her admirable soil. This appeal will be heeded and followed. For seven years, all races of humanity have been able to taste the joys of “home” while their brothers or fathers were fighting for "France". Today, those free of engine duty are free to traverse the long, white roads of France and witness the inimitable spectacle of French cities.

One of the most beautiful excursions one can make is that which, starting from Biarritz, on the Atlantic, leads you to Marseille on the Mediterranean: It is an excursion certain to satisfy even the most fanciful desires and to rejuvenate the taste of the most jaded. 

Some people will take a car in Europe this summer, but the majority of Americans will prefer not to encounter the difficulties that arise from importing automobiles into France. One can rent at Paris or Biarritz a good chauffeur and a good machine for a sum which does not exceed three to four francs per kilometer.

If the excursion is made starting from Paris, one has to reach Biarritz a direct and very beautiful route which traverses the region of the châteaux of the Loire, that delicious garden of France, Touraine, which is sprinkled with the most perfect masterpieces of the Renaissance; but those who desire to find themselves on the Riviera in autumn to take sun baths during the winter can commence their journey leisurely and comfortably over the thousand kilometers of the route.

Therefore, we depart from Biarritz; we choose September, which is the blessed month of this famous country; the French season is at its height: golf, tennis, bathing, dancing and all sorts of enjoyments succeed tumultuously in the most lively and contagious of frenzies. 

Through a country spared by war, far from battlefields and steeped in history, what a marvelous journey that from Biarritz to Marseille! Enthusiastic ease and particularities will lead them to bring their own for the introduction into this delightful garden. 

The hour has arrived to set out; here are the high peaks of the Pyrenees piercing through…

A cloudy sky, and the automobile speeds along the road to Pau. There are two routes to reach Pau; the shortest and most direct crosses Orthez but another skirts a region of more unsettling rocks, and the small village of Saint-Jean Pied-de-Port. One finds nothing modern in this little fortified town which commands a sombre gorge traversing the Pyrenees towards Spain: the Col de Roncevaux.

One hears as if the echo of armies on the march who crossed it in times past, and that brings out the gentle aerial tones of the Estes son and toine. From Saint-Jean Pied-de-Port, the road passes through graceful valleys and verdant meadows; picturesque, it passes within this adorable village where one sees the beautiful provincial bank: producers trail their small carts along the narrow paths.

The route becomes more arduous, difficulties arise at every instant; they are nothing but turns, nothing but ascents, and then soon the car arrives upon a smooth and white road. More than one hundred and fifty kilometers have already been traversed; there remain still a few, but one knows that a good dinner awaits you in the city which is not however part of Henri IV’s particular renown for its delectable French cuisine, for just now, at Saint-Jean Pied-de-Port, we savoured an inimitable meal composed of the most refined French dishes, and so it will be all along the road.

For the inn may be without pretension, the innkeeper may protest before you regarding the emptiness of his office and the desolation of his kitchen, but when it comes to setting table he will serve you a light bread, a well-browned chicken, savory vegetables and an old bottle from behind the fagots, all reaching such perfection that once the meal is swallowed it is impossible for it ever to leave your memory.

The peasants who work the land which descends towards Pau have tranquil brows; Pau is more tranquil than Biarritz; it is a city extremely English in character. The English organize fox hunts and horse races there; they have their particular clubs and their temples. Numerous historical memories arise in Pau, particularly within the old château where numerous kings of France and Béarn resided and which is now a museum full of relics.

Now, from Pau to Luchon, deep within the heart of the Pyrenees, it is merely a matter of one hundred kilometers; the route traverses (Continued on page 54) Saint-Jean Pied-de-Port evokes numerous legends.

Might it be due to its position at the entrance of that dark throat, Roncevaux which leads to Spain?

A fall of white houses with white roofs, old towers, a cathedral crowning the low hills and new ports along the banks of the river – such is Béziers. What joy it is to have luncheon or dinner in the open air beneath the shade of trees or under parasols, and what joy especially to savour the inimitable French cuisine!

From these admirable remains which have been passed down to us from Romanesque architecture, the theatre of Nîmes may well be the best preserved; one has simply reconstructed the gradins so as to be able to organize bullfights and cinematographic spectacles. 

One of the graces of the Basque villa of Saint-Jean Pied-de-Port lies in its cemetery with its tall poplars and its small houses, the glass which covers the tombs surrounded by flowers. 

If you prefer the road from Orthez to Saint-Jean Pied-de-Port, one enters this city through a bridge which is one of the two most curious fortified bridges that still exist.

A bathing costume of nattier blue cashmere, belted with white and accompanied by a kasha cape in white adds to the charm of the sea. Thus attired in a striped blue and white knitted canotier suit with a completely black bonnet, one may show oneself for an instant before diving.

She who wears wide canary yellow trousers with a black knitted body appears to desire to bathe without touching the water. I have seen, this Pacific country, a cold and humid land under a torrential rain, and the moments of sleep in the boat make me feel even more the contrast when I awaken in the small English port, under a brilliant sun and where railway employees are of a politeness and a calm that rests the brain, when I arrive at London, more fatigued than ever.

It is something else entirely: everywhere, sins, in the restaurants, there is a joie de vivre, almost abundance. She who has English revenues certainly has much more than before; hats, silk stockings; everything is more than affordable and above all of a marvelous quality. Taxis transport me from one end of London to the other for six shillings; restaurant bills are acceptable; only the apartment at the hotel costs dear, oh that, very dear! No doubt because there is congestion in London, a phenomenon which explains why life is so agreeable there.

During the "week end" that I spend at Norbiton, in a property of enchanting beauty, the pleasure increases; green lawns, in the immense house with old servants with white hair, well styled and so devoted to their masters, it is all quite natural; the luxury seems a thing of course; women are of surprising elegance. For playing croquet, for taking tea in the loggia decorated for that purpose, on the large tables with white tablecloths, served à la anglaise, what coquetry and refinement! Here it is Lady Cunard whose slender black gown is simple, but quite becoming. Her tiny foot is wonderfully shod in patent leather shoes with paws, each paw closed along the ankle and leg by a diamond buckle.

The Duchess Sangro in a blue silk dress with an immense matching hat, wears splendid gems upon her. Princess Obolenski, so beautiful beneath her enormous straw hat, wears a velvet gown with large leaves. Mrs. Dans la "Femme de mon ami" at the Théâtre Michel, Mademoiselle Huguette Dastry wears a Premet dress of cachemire green, a white pleated skirt edged with silk.

The narrow band that descends from the collar is embroidered in green and black.

After a brief sojourn in London, The Parisienne divides her evenings between the theatre and musical gatherings. What lovely costumes are displayed on stage! Customs officials, scrutinizing within the shops, it’s almost like a parade. One would wish to adorn one's friend with such finery, upon the blouse with an elegant air.

Miss Williams in white, a hat laden with grapes and apples, carries a Chinese parasol of silk in colour. The automobiles awaiting in the entrance court are all wonderfully maintained and of renowned make; the gardens are flowering as those of warm countries; everything, indeed, is paradisiacal. Add to this that each evening one is solicited by five or six balls; the theatre functions in both English and French; the grand hotels overflow with company. It is a very different impression from that experienced in Paris and which, I am certain, is due to that charming Anglo-Saxon optimism which remains one of the strengths of this people we must admire.

In a few days will take place the "blue ball" where, apart from all the women of the English aristocracy who will dance officially (since this ball is given for the benefit of a charitable cause), we expect from Paris some of our beautiful society stars such as the Duchess de Grammont who has promised to come and dance “one mata” with one of the principal dancers of the Russian troupe, currently in London.

Another evening, I dine at the home of one of our lovely Ladies; and as she is indisposed, we take a collation by her windowed salon, blossoming onto Hyde Park. There again, it is enchantment. She appears to me in a negligee embroidered with gold, an evocation of a Melisande’s adornment. On all the tables and upon the walls, there are only works of art and bibelots of very great value, while…

The English have a very special way of loving flowers: they do not place a bouquet of roses on their table; they have the entire salon flowering, on all the tables, on the mantels, upon the floor, before or at the angle of a table, the flowers burst forth like rockets; not only does the fragrance permeate the walls and hangings of a room, but for the eyes, the feast is immense. Not otherwise do they prick roses into their corsages? It was not a single rose, but a bush of roses that the lovely Lady who receives me wore at her waist.

Monsieur Premet was so delighted by Mademoiselle Dastry that he decided to make a cape to accompany it. The collar of one is closed by a large button.

A small white felt toque, completed with verdant plumes, enhances the ensemble. SO E marks the style, a development which is not to be overlooked when considering the accompanying robe. An entire creation designed to accompany her.

July I

In Paris, the fashionable life, though not as intense as during the last season, betrays a certain activity. Many musical mornings are taking place at present and when one has visited all the exquisite establishments which solicit us, nothing is more agreeable than to partake of refreshments in the calm of a charmingly arranged Home. That of Madame Granier is among the recent installations that must be noted, owing to the taste of M. Cuevas who has managed, for his compatriot, to find rare furnishings, those which antique dealers guard jealously for the favoured client. It is within this setting filled with lovely lacquered furniture, eighteenth-century pieces, and a very beautiful portrait by Beltram, the Spanish painter, that Madame Granier has hung her welcoming garland.

Yesterday, Monsieur Portal and M. Cuevas received several friends in their atelier on rue Magellan to hear the admirable cantatrice Mrs. Chater, whose voice enraptures the audience. 

At the Théâtre des Variétés, Mademoiselle Dorziat appeared first in a morning robe of Doucet, in grey suede, of an elegance beyond compare. Her tricorne of Reboux repeated the colour of the dress. The gilet and open collar of yellow contrasted delightfully. Mlle. Dorziat was composed for by Doucet a gown for evening wear in black lace and pearl embroidery with turquoise beads. The tunic is held by a belt of turquoise tulle tied very loosely. This ravishing toilette is accompanied by a cape of negre head satin adorned with fox fur, grand noir, and a blue cean fan.

In "Un Homme en habit," Mademoiselle Gabrielle acts in a robe de Borce in brown satin and gold lace with a cape adorned with black revers. Kubitsky then sang modern airs with charm and taste (Words by Apollinaire). 

The Princesse R., Mademoiselle d'Hinnisdal in rose, her turban grey, her dress cut as if from large petals. The Comtesse de Roche in a black gown embroidered with mother-of-pearl flowers. Castro in pale pink, tulle white skirt, very bouffante. Madame Ross in a black velvet gown, very décolletée.

At the Comte Poznanski’s, we heard this antiquated instrument, one might say “distant,” play the clavicord; its notes seem to come from beyond the centuries. The young Englishwoman who played this instrument in a salon lit only by candles, wearing a "surannée" gown of Louis XIII style, was dressed in grey and “infante.”

The bouffante, of a very typical air, with its large lace collar from which emerged a frail and rose-colored neck and a face evoking some ancient portrait. VOGUE
"THREE WEEKS IN MOROCCO"
By Pai

An immense need to wander, to forget the rights of suffering, draws us toward lands of light and dream, in order there to find solace. No place is better suited than Morocco for embracing the allure of Islam, with its nights warm and vibrant, living the past, the present; a tailor from Barclay and a hat from Georgette Claux – the principal attraction of Morocco, especially for the traveler, resides in the ease of means permitting travel. Our coquetry will be exercised there as everywhere: a thousand ingenious fancies will once more become reasons for charm, elegance, and seduction, whether lilies or enveloping furs, depending on whether we have chosen autumn or spring for this excursion; these two seasons being the only ones propitious for a motorcar journey in Morocco, where the railways are not to be recommended, the terrestrial network being far from complete. But thanks to the prodigious activity of the French protectorate, 2650 kilometers of good paved roads permit one to traverse this admirable country.

It is quite necessary to have a chauffeur of the country, speaking Arabic and knowing the tracks in case one should be tempted to try one. The tracks are passable only during the favorable seasons in order to avoid the mud of the rainy seasons or the sand of the drought, enemies of the tourist; two risks particularly to be feared between Tangier and Kénitra. A track traversing the Spanish zone where the native, not very welcoming, can provoke a thousand unpleasant troubles which we ourselves have experienced.

Three itineraries were proposed to us from Paris: “Paris-Marseille-Tangier,” requiring three days of travel, boat included; these were not as agreeable as the crossing of Spain, which offered us a charming introduction to the art and landscapes of that land. The third, "Bordeaux-Casablanca" without stopover, seemed destined for our return. “Irun-Madrid-Algésiras” therefore took place one evening around five o’clock, departing from Austerlitz. This penetrating humidity, atrocious in a Paris of January, made us taste perhaps even better the joy of a departure toward the sun. Comfortably enveloped in our beaver and small-grey pelisses, we thought of abandoning them soon. A dark green harmonizing with the stripe of the same tone as the classic and neat costume, and the silk sweater –

A veil of smoky lace feminizes the ensemble somewhat; we read a few books by Berthe Georges Gaulis. "France in Morocco."

We awaken in Irun, where the express train to Madrid, having departed without waiting for that of Paris, obliges us to spend the day awaiting the train to St. Sébasthien, and arrive the following day in Madrid. A day at the Ritz and departure for Algesiras, where we find the long-awaited sun. A land of dreams, of repose. Cristina, very English, provides an exclusive comfort within the loveliest of gardens. Lennis Jettent the white sheen of their costumes into the raw green of the palms: the balls too, rebound upon a soil. The marvelous lamp of Aladdin – it is the automobile that conducts the fervent traveler to the land of new delights: Morocco, the country of a thousand legends. It seems as though these latter years have left behind traces of sadness, but that they are now somewhat embraced by magic.

It offers us all the curative magic of the Orient, all the poetry of landscapes infinitely variable, rapidly changing within the confines of the land. One regrets the unpredictable nature of breakdowns without hope. Five to six – we cannot hold onto time. “Paris-Bor-” We were obliged to leave Orsay flooded. The leather hat, among others "la" - the excellent hotel Reina – players of a reddish hue, admirable in tone, already African, of great charm, raw from its sky and the ardent red of its earth, and seems to wish to reserve for itself alone the adornment of vivid colours.

One must dress there in white or neutral tones so that the colours do not clash with the sky and the earth, but of demi-robes. They wear at this hour, a suit purchased en passant in Madrid. After three days of repose, departure via Gibraltar with the comfortable English Daleau, to arrive at Tangier, an international port where French and Spanish have not yet built a true port...

Upon disembarking at Tangier in a small boat, the restless sea welcomes us by inundating us, but fortunately our Arab guide is there. Our luggage, from the hotel, from the automobile which will tomorrow take us from Tangier to Rabat, but permits only one simple item as baggage within the car. At the comfortable and very simple hotel, the travel suit is exchanged for a costume and tailleur de voyage.

Beside the ancient mosque, the Medersa of Bon-Ananya at Fez serves as a market for the vendors of the bazaar and as a study hall for the students of the old university – a magnificent contrast of blue. At the hotel, one dresses in the evening. A few elegant women wear a Manton de Manila. 



PAR LA COMTESSE DE SAINT-SAUVEUR

Mohamed, who attends to everything, from the valise for each person, to the reception at the residence of General and Madame Lyautey, always so welcoming to those who traverse the protectorate. From Tangier to Kénitra, the journey across the track is one of great difficulty; our automobile is the first this season to have ventured there.

It is necessary to leave Tangier at five in the morning, in order to sleep in Rabat by evening; the road is not long, but it resembles more a ploughed field where with each turn of the wheel one risks becoming bogged down. There are bridges over the Oueds (rivers), and in one of them the rear wheels of the car sink – a breakdown! There are natives who lend a helping hand for a few douros, but the native is rather hostile to foreigners; fortunately, a small troop of Spanish soldiers pass by with horses, which the effort of arms had not managed.

Finally, the automobile departs again and the race resumes in the wild rif, where flowers dot the ground, but one must be wary of them as they conceal a formidable mud. We traverse Larache, then we cross the frontier after a stop of two hours in an Arab village composed of a dozen tents. (Continued on page 50)

A town suit, certainly, but from this first day in Moroccan soil, it will never again be more than a town suit, fashioned or unfashioned, warm, but always accompanied by a silk sweater or fine wool. For the evening only, the décolleté gown has its place for dinner at the hotel, but the suit remains the order of the day.

What a contrast with the Comtesse de Sauveur, dressed in the latest mode, and this admirable native bearing the draped mantle that was worn two thousand years ago! Less than half the place is realised, their horses are attatched to the automobile, where the effort of arms had not succeeded.

"THE BOAT AND SEALING WAX"
27

Here is a trousseau of keys to open a mysterious casket and a thread of Ariadne to guide us through the secret drawers of an old bureau.

Among the childhood memories that rise within my heart, in my mature years, I evoke principally a chamber where I had a boat, an ivory boat which was found enclosed within a glass box placed upon a table; upon the deck of this boat rose a fantastic dais beneath which Cleopatra stretched out her beautiful body for Antony, leaning over her breast, to contemplate in her wide eyes stars of golden points "an entire immense sea where galleys fled."

The lines of this boat, its cut, the arabesque of its stern, the filigree assembled—all made up an ensemble that rejoiced the soul and caused me to utter cries of joy before this boat which embodied for me the great intoxication of departures. A piece of ivory could suggest that this piece was a lacquered beam fallen from its edge and floating upon the transparent sea.

It is a curious coincidence, undoubtedly, but this boat and this sealing wax have struck my mind as a symbolic vision of remarkable clarity, which, in my opinion, is indispensable to discourse, gesture, and written phrase. And rightly, against affectation; but for some time now there has been a tendency toward negligence in the intellectual domain: language is enameled with slang words, gestures have taken on an ugly air, and one has written only in jargon. These things have intertwined with frenzy, cacophony, and awkwardness, which are certain signs of intellectual decay. Intelligence, enclosed within itself, with a vigorous framework, that the present movement—a princess of legend held under a diabolical charm—has shaken.

The boat has always been for me the type of the most beautiful movements, the symbol of true elegance in style and gesture, because there is nothing superfluous upon a ship. Sealing wax is also naturally a symbol of reticences, of things one wishes to keep secret; secrets it is beautiful to hold closest. One will naturally think of classical Greece to find an expression of this constraint, this moderation in the translation of life but it is charming to recall what was once found there—the charm of its masts, all these exquisite things that have always brought forth within me a vision of something hidden.

One has written much generally about bringing a general correction to language; yet, intelligence, in general, shows itself to be lacking.

A life organized, it seals voluntarily, a red word; one uses sealing wax. The word has taken itself into a body and is free, while life suits the profound depths of oneself. Perhaps there’s no need to go so far to understand what I am trying to express; there remains a tradition at the present time whose roots are not dead but merely tend to become etiolated.

Let us gather in our minds the boat and the sealing wax, the inkwell and its apple-green tray, the feather duster of horsehair, the small boxes adorned with delicate gold filigrees containing the coloured wafers, the blues, lilacs, geraniums, lemons and let us join to these the laquered black blotting stamp, inlaid with Chinese emblems in mother-of-pearl and goose feathers. All these objects bathe in a delicate atmosphere; a slender clock of gold, tranquil; an aromatic air wafts like lavender from a linen cupboard slightly ajar where familiar scents are contained, a scent which perhaps ignores the brutalities of life but which holds countless sensibilities and resonances for those delicate souls who do not merely roar the word "magic" at the admirable ideal of the past.

It was in this atmosphere that letters were once written, with an Italian hand, fragile and slanting, letters from Priscilla to John who gnawed his heart, “Priscilla te my darling ummeline” who lived in her exquisite country house at Chiswick and who travelled via the Simplon Pass to the Italian lakes in her "barouche" with her mother and father whose long faces were adorned with moustaches.... These were letters, truly full of caressing intimacy which flourished in retirement but whose scent still lingers within us in our old age like the scent of a faded fan held by an adored hand, a fragrance that those who wish to contemplate it would perfume.

Let us not proclaim a frantic admiration for this delicious Second Empire era with its follies and its futilities. God preserve us from them! 

Then, at that charming epoch, in the small things of life, there was a reserve, a skillful sense which contributed to an impression of security and repose in existence: and why, indeed, should that disappear, even though the manner of expressing it has changed?

We must keep our “boats and sealing wax” as a talisman, for certain dangerous natures want to tear us away from all gentleness; will we not surround the soul with a triple magic circle, will we not find…

means of defending ourselves between those who mount the assault on our culture, will we not find the incantation that can drive these away, far from us, with their discordant cries...?

It is as if a garment were to detach itself from an armoire, a symbol of progress, but which renders the man who lived in his own dust, vanished for our spirits.

There is in the house of Monsieur Charles Sabin, at Southampton, a charming porch with bare walls adorned with plants and furnished with wicker armchairs, sofas in grey blue willow, lip pockets, and a charming and essential place within a country house one could scarcely imagine now without a porch. It has been only a short time that porches have been designed as we see them now; until these last years they consisted simply of a slight projection from the house; recently they have become something more than the shelter of two or three chairs, a pretension. The modern idea of a porch is limited only by dictates of elegance and comfort; it is the place where one is happiest to spend charming hours stretched upon a chaise longue, where one can best savour favourite landscapes glimpsed between arches or columns, where one can comfortably enjoy the book one prefers, nestled within the cushions of a deep armchair, with on one’s side a small table, glasses filled with bacees and barglacees, and friends who surround you.

There are naturally good ways and bad ways to organise a porch; the first condition to observe is that it must appear to be an integral part of the house; nothing is more unsightly than a porch which seems added. There is an infinite variety in decorating, furnishing, organising it, giving it an allure so that it marries with the house and with the garden. It is charming when the garden appears to continue into the porch and as it were within it; one can paint the loggia roof in dark blue and adorn it with stars and signs of the zodiac in gold; the chaise longues are painted in mauve and blue and upholstered in mauve, while the tents are tapissées en bleu. The colours mauve and blue are a theme which should also dominate in the garden; these are shades that assort with a house of neutral colour; Venetian canvas is also pretty to serve for making the tents and window draperies.

Where do they come from? One knows not. Women display the allure of elephants and wear rings on their index fingers, while men sport bull’s-neck collars and boots that make them totter. Children dab at their noses. One thinks, upon seeing them, of certain official galas and regrets that these have remained confined to the Elysée Palace balls where they would undoubtedly make a fine showing.

Alas! They have invaded our theatres, our restaurants, our promenades, and the Parisian of before the war has the astonishment of an émigré returning from Coblentz after the Terror. He looks, rubs his eyes, looks again, and cannot unravel what surprises him so greatly. Everything seems to remain in its place; nevertheless, it appears that everything has changed. What, pray tell, has happened?

Faithful to his habits, the Parisian goes to seek the cool air around the Place Vendôme and, a curious thing, finds he no longer recognizes anyone. A great many people, but a motley and bizarre crowd in soft hats, travelling hither and thither; the Parisian is uneasy, shocked. He scrutinizes the shops, inspects the interiors of automobiles, and despite his constancy, does not perceive a single face worthy of a tip of the hat.

Alarmed, he makes his way to the Bois de Boulogne where this time he truly seems to be in a lost country. A coupé from which descends an elderly lady with her little dog, two old gentlemen who discuss matters gravely, a young man awaiting beneath a tree someone who will not arrive—and that is all, absolutely all.

Ah! Some riders! An Amazon appears, dressed like a trained dog and mounted astride a circus horse. A gentleman of the masculine persuasion accompanies her, coiffed in a pointed hat and shod in boots as if he were asking, “What is this?” Eusèbe, the model of servants, the only familiar figure that remains in Paris, will accompany Monsieur le Comte to plant cabbages in the countryside.

Monsieur le Comte is astonished; impeccable service for the most perfect dinners are now invaded by individuals with bull’s-neck collars and children who dab at their noses.

The entrance of clowns and a judge have led him to believe that the Administration du Bois should perhaps pay more attention to the attire of strollers and their manner of riding. But amidst his reflections, he observes that the old lady has returned to her car, the elderly gentlemen have disappeared into the undergrowth, and, weary of waiting, the young man himself has vanished.

A great sadness invades the heart of the Parisian, no less than the pressing desire to flee this place of desolation. He seeks a taxi, sees none, and when he does spot one, the drivers seem determined to ignore him. The Parisian is scandalized, filled with righteous indignation. More melancholy, he resumes on foot in the direction of regions he hopes will be less hostile, and muses that since 1914 life has not become comfortable nor joyful.

Still, he is hungry, and cheered by the prospect of sitting before a white tablecloth, he enters a restaurant. The restaurant is full, and, to make matters worse, full of people he does not know. It feels like an intentional slight. He turns toward a neighboring establishment, only to find himself once again confronted with the same restaurants—celebrated establishments or others—a wearying repetition.

Weary of war and further disheartened, he exclaims: “Goodness! The restaurant is packed!” It’s a trial indeed. In his haste, he reaches the house of domestics; meanwhile, the rain falls. My God! How disappointing it all is, and how at certain hours one feels the need to weep! (The Parisian detests solitude.)

Come now, a final effort. He gains the Avenue de l'Opéra, enters an illustrious purveyor, this time too encountering an inhospitable crowd, eclipsed. As he reaches the door, suddenly someone clutches his coat and calls him by name in a supplicating tone: “Monsieur le Comte is not going away! It has been so long since we have seen Monsieur le Comte!”

He recognizes Eusèbe. Eusèbe, model of servants and doyen of the establishment’s boys. A flood of memories rushes into his mind, and as in days gone by, how much amusement they had! Eusèbe, despite the years, has remained steadfast at his post, and Eusèbe has not changed (he was already old in 1900); always dignified, freshly shaved, with that single lock of hair which he methodically winds around his bald and gleaming head.

Individuals appear in décolletages resembling bulls’ horns, causing them discomfort, and some insist on wiping their noses with their fingers. From cabaret to cabaret, the Parisian seeks an asylum where he might sit down and wonders if he will not finally die of hunger. The street is now deserted, before a hall overrun by a crowd; he prepares to return to his name and a supplicating tone: “Monsieur le Comte is going away? Oh!” Then the Parisian turns around.

This honest face evokes a Parisian—finally, a friendly figure, he finds himself anew in the land of his birth, reborn in Paris. Respectable Eusèbe! Before him, the heart of the Parisian was not quite free from a certain cursed self-love; he would fall into paternal reverie, and one hears him exclaim, "Eusèbe, Eusèbe, my old branch, would it be indiscreet to ask you to dine? I have been for an hour everywhere dreaming of lace."

Eusèbe relieves the newly arrived gentleman of his cane and his hat. Monsieur le Comte is excused. We must not vex Monsieur le Comte! For since Paris has become a veritable place of wisdom, the true sagacity consists in retiring, far from the world, into the solitude of the botperqui.

And indeed, the Parisian finds a table awaiting him, his usual table, down there, beneath the staircase, in the very spot where violins were wont to make their joyous clamour. He sighs with relief and, lifting his eyes, perceives Eusebe who, pencil in hand, poised like a soldier, awaits the order. “Make your own menu,” replies Eusebe with assurance. 

A dozen Petit perdail and the Sa, retephe – Eusebe goes away, returns, hurries on: "What are all these people? Everyone! In the streets, an abominable crowd, and not one decent soul amongst them. The restaurants are crowded, and I no longer find a single familiar face! — Clients, there is no lack of clients; whatever you desire, it’s all the same. Evenings, for persons like us, there are no more persons like us. One doesn't know where they come from.”

In this foreign Paris, Monsieur le Comte remembers the first time he escaped from his paternal home by slipping down the staircase. When the beautiful days return, having become kings once more, Monsieur le Comte and his faithful Eusebe will again inhale the air of the capital gaily along the Avenue du Bois. He unfolds his napkin. “My faith, Eusebe, you have good memory.”

“Oh! I remember,” Eusebe replies, "a dozen oysters, that’s all!” There isn't a cat in sight at the restaurants. The remainder – there are clients; it is not they who are lacking. “What do you want?” It’s all the same. For people like us, one no longer has people like us. 

Monsieur le Comte recalls? Twenty Gods! How Monsieur le Comte amused himself! He remembers the day Eusebe served him his first bottle of champagne, a memorable occasion that returns to them both with long hair and beards of eight days, men of politics, profiteers, unfortunate souls who immediately thrust fifty francs in gratuity upon you!”

“Fifty francs!” cries Eusebe, raising his shoulders. “Oh! I had no need of this, nothing like it before the war without these disastrous pursuits. Only, I am a winner; it gives me good times.” (Eusèbe sighs) "It is all equal." Monsieur le Comte recalls? 

At this moment, Eusebe straightens himself: "You must make a dame play!" There had been Monsieur le Prince d'Armagne, with Mlle Follebiche du Gymnase, and also Mlle Yvonne Lainaire. All, Monsieur le Comte and his friends arrived for dinner.

Here, everyone knew one another. Following this, they would go to the theatre, and then return together for supper. It is enough to say that one saw only them, and that, every night, the music played until late!

It was worse still with the Parisian: Eusèbe, it’s true we laughed a great deal. I remember the day when I made my début in that house. I was studying rhetoric and had escaped from my paternal home to be on service. I absorbed a bottle of Champagne, and although it cost dear today, I became my poor aunt and led, as they said then, a life guided by others.

Brillante Eusèbe, an incomparable age. In the morning, we drove together. (Continued on page 55) Even the Bois, which was once the theatre of the most elegant life, has become a wild place; among all the women one encounters there, one never finds the one one would truly wish to see.

Date mémorable. It was through your kindness that I inherited my first home, and it was by filting down the staircase that I absorbed the life at its grandest epoch.

There are many reports of Aubusson carpets, which were made in France during the eighteenth century, and flowered Persian rugs that were glazed in England at the same epoch. It seems that the artistic sense guided the landscape designers of both countries. The Persian rugs of this period were covered with simple, childlike flowers, as one finds in the gardens of England, while the Aubusson carpets were decorated and delicately knotted, presided over by admirable methods which now are frequently united in the most beautiful salons of England and also those of America.

One who reads the novels of George Moore, Walpole or Compton—these renowned writers—is certain, one day or another, to be transported into the atmosphere of a salon filled with Aubusson carpets, flowering Persian rugs, charming the spirit with the gentle brilliance of these treasures. Nowhere does one find so many colours as in the houses of London, perhaps because of those terrible fogs against which the Persians and Aubussons are like an eternal protestation.

The English people have such a love for the soul of gardens that they create as much as possible, both in town and country, an unreal atmosphere; they wish to see again, within the city, the image of the flowers they love, upon the Persian rugs which cover furniture and walls.

ENGLISH PERSIANS
THEIR ENGLISH CHARM

Those who do not care for the use of flowering Persian carpets in a chamber would certainly change their opinion if they could see one of these numerous rooms in England; they seem to revive all the gardens of that country: the green carpet is like an emerald wall, and from the hanging Persian rugs which form a background to books, engravings, and countless mirrors, innumerable bouquets of flowers are added. These bouquets are covered with dew, which serves as the adornment of the English salon; nowhere does one see flowers as in London, nowhere is there such prodigality, and it is a custom as established as that of the five o’clock tea.

In America, the glazed Persian is as common as it is currently in England, for one cannot imagine England without a glazed Persian, nor France without toile de Jouy. All the old Persians which one finds everywhere—the gay colours of these old Persians, the flowered designs

Harmonious Aubusson carpets bloom deliciously upon the wall hangings, curtains and parquet floors.

These two bouquets, spaced harmoniously, are bordered with gold. The reader of Hugh Mackenzie will find them particularly appreciated for reading or dreaming as he pleases. From the pond covered with water lilies, one can see reasserted presence and flowerbeds of brilliant hues. It does not seem possible to avoid entering directly into a garden in the manner of a geometric design. To penetrate it, a progressive path from the house is preferable; this axiom is most charmingly demonstrated by the garden of Doctor Henry Lancashire at Manchester, in the United States.

From the grassy terrace which lies before the house, to the terrace supported by a stone wall, underlined by pottery vases, one progressively passes through lawns that ascend to the level of the garden; these lawns are decorated with diverse masses of colored flowers according to the seasons.

Standing on the terrace before the house, one sees the entire garden and the trees above which lead to a semi-circular pond covered with green water lilies in clear water. At this point, the path divides. On either side, paths covered with gravel lead to a pergola so thickly covered with Virginia creeper that one might wonder if it is truly a pergola, and there the harmonious garden terminates.

All around, a landscape filled with chaotic rocks and verdant trees. The garden thus is a multicolored jewel; its irregular lines, its multiple colorations contrast with the wild character of the surrounding environment.

A HOUSE FOR A LONG GARDEN
on the Longmeade estate, on the road to Madingley, near Cambridge, is a very happy and very particular example of the new models of English domestic architecture. The applications of these principles in houses are often moderated, for it is still easy to make an elegant house, practical and expending much artistry, but it is far more difficult to obtain the same result by spending little. Likewise, questions of terrain are very important; certain terrains lend themselves more or less to the practical disposition of a house. One can readily appreciate these two points in studying the nature of the problem as it has been resolved in the house we represent here for the readers of Vogue.

The name Longfield (long field) perfectly characterizes the aspect of the terrain for which the house was constructed. The site is, literally, a long field, one extremity touching the road to Madingley. From the other side, the field extends into the countryside over a fairly long space, but it is scarcely wider than the house that is built upon it. Being limited thus by the narrowness of the terrain—a capital defect—it was necessary to design the house in such a way that it might be as far removed as possible from the dust deposited by carriages on the road, and that the garden should be arranged in an agreeable fashion.

One enters first through a charming path which runs along one side of the gardens, while the remainder of the width of the property, extending from the road to the kitchen garden, serves as a transition to a small esplanade placed before the north or side entrance of the house. The house extends across the entire width of the property as we have said; it divides the property into two parts and is a protective barrier behind which the flower-filled garden stretches with its gay colours.

ARCHITECTURAL STYLE
This house follows, as architectural style, the old local traditions of the countryside. One can find its prototype in all the environs among the numerous manors that still grace this region, some dating back to the fifteenth century. WHAT ONE SEES IN THE SHOPS

It is, indeed, more necessary in matters of fashion that one adhere to the dictates of good taste than it is for bathing costumes; both in the selection of colours and in the choice of designs. Atrocities have frequently been perpetrated by those who manufacture these sorts of garments, both as regards their purchase and the manner in which they are worn: for the bathing costume is the garment that one wears in public wherein one displays the greatest amount of nudity and the least possible fabric; it is indispensable that a refined taste correct these two extremes and that its designs be as simple as its colours are calm.

The most cultivated women, those who possess the best education, favour black or marine blue; those of a “Negro head” effect are one very graceful sight, but when they stain, they are easily marked, and the same reproach may be levelled at costumes with broad bands of vivid colour. However, narrow trimmings in neutral tones or in white add a tranquil charm and without exaggeration to bathing costumes.

FOR THE BATHING GIRL

Observe, for example, the coloured trimmings which produce a truly charming effect on the black satin costume depicted amidst the group below; they emphasize the lower portion of the garment, the necklines and armholes, and simulate a lace trimming upon the bodice. Cut in a very simple fashion, with a belt that breaks the line, this costume is entirely well-conceived; it is, in short, the most practical for a woman who swims for real.

I July

ELEGANCE FOR THE SMALLER FIGURE

This foulard dress, suggested for travel, gives an impression of freshness. It is dark blue with white crêpe georgette accents.

Now that Europe is once again capable of devoting its attention to the normal things in life… and taking on a little of the spirit of the time of peace, it opens wide its doors to travellers. This summer it seems there must be a general exodus from the United States towards the continent, an exodus which for some will be a source of pleasure, and for others a respectful pilgrimage to devastated lands. On the other hand, one notices in the United States itself a veritable rage for displacement – formerly a privilege judged to reign over the vast consumer, but today even the wealthy and those with limited incomes are particularly desirous of appearing at their best when travelling.

Thus she chooses her most elegant tailor suit. Tweeds and tartans have suggested the cape we see here. The fabric is sufficiently thick; it need not be lined, although a silk lining is always chic. Travelling coats and dresses can be very practical without losing any of their elegance and she will choose with her turban and veil the most becoming.

For long journeys, the woman with limited means must organize herself to account for difficulties; she chooses a dress adorned at the collar and sleeves with elegant lingerie, and it would be wise to have several such adornments which should, moreover, be as simple as possible so as to be her own chambermaid. The woman favours the dress over the tailor suit, and as soon as she considers the problem of the blouse, victory goes to the serge or light-fabric tailor dress.

One of these serge dresses is reproduced below and on page 47. For travel or for town, it is simply adorned with waxed braid or ribbon and fabric buttons. The braid forms a flat bow at the nape of the neck. The demi-long sleeves may be pleated in organdi, frilled in crêpe georgette or gathered in tulle, as well as simple hemmed bands held at the cuffs by black ribbon which passes transparently through the hem and forms a bow. A piece of lingerie is also frilled on black ribbon.

Charming but very practical and requiring little time to make, one meter of tulle will produce two adornments. It is also very easy to launder. 

For travel in warm weather, sleeves

Of fabric sewn onto a detachable background may be replaced by others in lighter fabrics if they are fashionable this season, such as light checked fabrics or large checks, organdies, white batistes, or even plain crêpe georgette which…

This cape of marine blue serge, flannel anglaise cream, or silk, according to whether one desires it more or less warm, lends itself to the chic of a wardrobe while allowing for the ease of blanchissage. In the case where she would be forced into reduced circumstances and economy, it is very practical – a gilet; these sleeves are finished at the top and bottom with elastic.

This ensemble is not only simple, but is lined with warm fabric, so that if she wishes to carry it away or share it, it will retain its charm. But for those who prefer lightness, the crêpe de Chine is always fresh and convenient for the city and for short journeys. The hand-drawn designs are beige or blue.

Bags – these dresses adorned with them can all be bleached easily. With several of these guimpes, a robe is always fresh, an advantage considerable during the heatwave. An elegant little cape accompanying this dress reproduced at the bottom of page 47 is decidedly fashionable; simple, lined with plain taffeta or flannel anglaise cream, or even tussor.

A great richness is displayed in the thick, folded Scottish striped tweeds and in the wool fabrics of this season, and the cape that one sees to the left, on page 47, is made from one of these fabrics. It would be chic and very comfortable for the lower part of the body; lined if the fabric is not sufficiently heavy, or lined with flannel or tussor. With it harmonizes a turban draped in the same fabric. (Continued on page 55)

This charming travelling dress in serge is adorned with waxed braid or ribbon. The gilet and the lower sleeves are of net, which gives the dress a delicious and chic cachet. Very simple, and so it is!

Madame, when one finds oneself in such an atmosphere, one desires a very practical plane on which aviators can remain indefinitely; one would wish to halt time and prevent the sun from setting, and yet what beauty is a sunset viewed from an aeroplane! The clouds float over the countryside, in the gentleness of twilight; the last rays of light disappear behind the mountains or are drowned in the immensity of the ocean, in that exquisite hour...!

And who could render the prodigious aspect of the clouds one contemplates now above, and now below oneself? They are like a curtain which would show the lining when seen from below, for they are dark grey; but one traverses them, one surmounts their cottony mass and then one beholds the most Claude Purner has ever attempted to translate, and it is beneath a dome so wonderfully blue that a cluster of hills appears, seemingly transparent, reflecting all the colours of the rainbow.

A TERRIBLE HABIT
Experienced aviatrices will notice that while their first ascent afforded them joy, they aspired after the second, needed the third, and the fourth time in an aeroplane; it seems one is a bird and has, like him, the need for high altitudes; one then desires to have one’s own aeroplane, an aeroplane which allows you to travel to Egypt to spend the winter, or even, if necessary, into the heart of the Sahara, as once one would have gone to spend eight days at Fontainebleau.

Fortunately, and although the automobile industry is in its beginnings, there are aeroplanes costing 2,000 dollars, and which are a small aeroplane advanced... (Continued from page 6)

American and Canadian students receive their instruction up to “The Eagle,” costing 40,000. This accommodates seven passengers and offers modern comfort, even including a perfectly appointed dressing room; the passengers can circulate between the seats far more easily than they could change places in a sumptuous Rolls-Royce on the avenue du Bois. One may sit beside the window while travelling at a speed of over 200 kilometers per hour, for the windows have been established by engineers at just the point of departure from her gown.

The external pressure and the internal pressure. LAigle possesses three engines; and if, by chance, a fortuit Lorrain accident were to befall the engines, the pilot can keep his smile and content himself with landing a little earlier for lunch.

Between the “J. N.” and the “Aigle” there are all sorts of intermediary machines; for example, the "Loriot" is a three-passenger aeroplane which we cannot recommend too highly to brunettes whose complexion will harmonize with it. The "Loriot," this second aeroplane, Orville Wright, for women who want to strike a pose (and I must admit that there were some) has just had constructed an aero-coupé of astonishing chic. There are also the giants Handley-Page which can lift seventeen passengers and are very practical for numerous excursions into the countryside. A seaplane could surpass the "Goëland" which is capable of accomplishing voyages at a speed of five hundred and sixty kilometers, yet with a velocity still at its own discretion; you can with a “Goeland” fly from the Seine, you can alight in the country—it is a limousine possessing all the attributes that the chic woman must have. One may even attach a fur-trimmed mantle to it with straps to the belt and the sides of the bodice, thus ravishing, in short, one’s admirers, whether at one or even two speeds, with its fuselage.

You can fly six hundred kilometers at a speed of 150 kilometers per hour. See page 52. This couture is a marvel; this tunic bordered with fur can be fastened with straps to the belt and to the sides of the bodice.

“THREE WEEKS IN MOROCCO”

We find ourselves in a land sheltering indigenous families so backward that we can scarcely believe it, especially the women, who wear white but soiled garments and carry their children on their backs wrapped in a strip of cloth which secures them firmly. We arrive at Kénitra to dine in a very rudimentary fashion; then we discover the French road so well arranged and maintained by the protectorate that we roll along at full speed. We finally arrive at Rabat where the Hotel de la Tour Hassan will offer us a well-deserved rest. Disease operates here as elsewhere, and without the precaution of having received telegraphic confirmation regarding the availability of rooms, we should be without lodging.

At Rabat, there is no disillusionment to fear; the old civilization envelops you from your arrival; the past revives and we feel all the difference between this journey and those accomplished previously—not merely for the landscapes which seduce, but for the very soul that palpitates and lives within the walls of Rabat-la-Rouge. Salé-la-Blanche, the Chellah or Garden of the Dead, evoke before us a whole past of wars and religion. The entire feudalism seems to revive here.

and the contrast is all the more striking with the prodigious and so modern activity of the governmental direction of the protectorate. Rabat was built in the time of Philippe III by the Spanish Moors who found themselves, their descendants forming still the very closed noble caste. The Tour Hassan, sister to the Giralda of Seville and the Koutoubia of Marrakech, allows us well to understand the intimate union which existed at that epoch between the Peninsula and this land of Africa.

The Kasbah des Oudayas rises opposite Salé, a formidable defense where women and children were sheltered during the bloody struggles. It evokes a cult imbued with so much peace and grandeur that the traveler is seized, impressed, comprehending that whatever it may be, something subsists there, outside of him, outside of his time, and this impression will remain forever in his spirit as the most captivating of memories.

Comprehending all that passes, whether warrior or profoundly psychological, concerning the General Lyautey, his tact, his finesse to rally to the cause – the Corsairs of Salé, the great Caïds of Marrakech, the rich merchants of Fez, so many cities, so many diverse souls to understand and to win. We shall no longer be surprised by the result obtained by the General when we have the honour of dining with him at Rabat, hive of activity, centre of French culture in Morocco, where a perfect understanding of art has intelligently conserved the admirable part that passed alongside the economic modern.

In the traveling trunk of the Comtesse de Saint-Sauveur was found this négligé from Charvet in apricot silk, very simple but very practical for… (Continued from page 22)

After a monotonous route of three hundred kilometers, biblical caravans and we arrive at the site of the famous battle of Sidi-Ben-Otman where the General Mangin definitively affirmed Marrakech and opened to us the doors of the Atlas. We traverse the restful Palmeraie. In the distance, the Koutoubia soars towards the blue sky above the city.

Further still, the Atlas with its eternal snows fades away, concealing from view the Sahara, deep and mysterious. We inhabit the Arab city where, on the square, storytellers evoke before a collected and solemn public…

The women of the impenetrable land. The young boys, clad in white, dance to the monotone music, and the active and numerous merchants barter ceaselessly. It is the great silence from which rise the chants of the Muezzins.

One must visit the Menara, a pavilion of repose for the Sultans before which shimmers a large basin, and where orange trees laden with fruit, entwined with jasmine and clematis, create of this place a dreamlike setting. We are drawn to the beautiful Sahadiens, where El Mansour, conqueror of the Sudan, rests near the sultans in the Mosque constructed in 159L.

After a visit to the Baïha, residence of General Lyautey, we dine at the Subdivision, of the Service de Renseignements. Here is a pretty Persian rug with blue ribbon bows, red and rose ribbons in wild roses on a sapphire ground. The old flowers of our gardens – the hibiscus, like the jasmine and magnolia – were also favourite designs amongst all, but the mixtures of flowers of every species and every colour on a white background, the whole giving an exquisite impression of freshness, contributed greatly to the success of glazed Persians in England. It is thanks to the ease with which one could wash and press them as ordinary linen; it is quite contrary to iron a Persian rug in America, where one must have a special machine that applies starch perfectly over the entire surface; however, it is possible to possess a glazed Persian and keep it with its original appearance for a period which can exceed two years without having to wash it if the dust is regularly wiped from the smooth surface.

In all old documents relating to that time, constant mention is made of bedspreads of Persian rugs, covers and rugs, which proves the interest our ancestors showed in them. 

A LIBRARY OF UNCOMMON CHARM
A wonderful collection of blue-grey Persian hangings was discovered last summer in an old Irish manor at Port Arlington. These hangings are of a delicious colour; large Chinese flowers in blue on a lighter sky blue amidst leaves and branches of a greyish green form a veritable poem of colours. These charming hangings now adorn the walls of a small dining room; they are fortunately matched with an Aubusson carpet and chairs covered with another glazed Persian. The wooden panels of the walls are painted cream colour, and on the carpet bouquets of flowers are drawn on a dark green background; the mahogany table is old Sheraton style, and the chairs which reproduce the French style called Saint-Cloud, are painted in blue and covered with black glazed Persian striped with white, scattered with bouquets of flowers. Flowers still adorn this room, flowers in cups and vases, plants flourish in red vases.

There is a library in New York, of English style, where glazed Persians marry in the most charming way with furnishings that seem worthy, with medallions on a pale green background. 
(Continued from page 36)

The proprietor guided the decorator so that he might compose for him a room of very used, yet different, objects – a sombre library. It is a white room with very simple moldings in style; three spaces between the windows are filled by the library; at the windows, dormer-like projections display Persian rugs from England decorated with flowers where all the shades of pink, red, and greens appear on a white background. For this purpose, a Persian rug covers a large sofa near the fireplace; this rug, which is quite literally the least costly thing one can imagine, constitutes the motif, the true decorative base of the room; furthermore, one sees there a carpet of taupe color; before the fire, a small Aubusson floral carpet; the mantelpiece of the chimney is in old wood decorated with garlands of flowers, a nuance barely more accentuated than the natural color of the wood. A screen of satin reproduces the green of the Persian rug; made from an ancient bedspread and charmingly suggests the vision of a hedge in a very old garden. Large spaces are arranged on either side of the chimney and on the opposite wall where books take up the most space. Old Venetian glassware there scintillates gently; there are, of course, numerous lamps spread throughout the room for convenience, but the soft glow of these lends charm to this library and creates an exquisite milieu for conversation and confidences. Some notes, and a clear green, give the room a joyful and virile aspect; it is thus that the curtains are held back by narrow red ribbons; the superb portrait of one of Napoleon’s marshals wearing a red coat gives a martial note and makes the faded bindings of the old books stand out in comparison. The green nuance is found not only on the screen but also on the secretary, its gilt patina sparkling, and whose doors are… Open, the desk is of a red and gold hue, harmonizing with the ensemble of the room; one sees that this library is of perfect rhythm; everything is in its place, where it ought to be, and one could not remove anything without destroying all its harmony! Harting, from a museum, has lent a piece possible of the usual habit. The result illuminates the windows through large openings sown with leaves. A magnificent Venetian lamp, this green spot, combines with lustres and sconces in candles which contribute to the atmosphere of a brilliant red Venice laquered in green; troubled glasses harmonize in perfection. “MADAME, THE AEROPLANE IS” – whether at Dinard or at Marseille, you can…

To pursue the shadow-knight, to go fishing – whether at Annecy or to shoot wildfowl on the lake of Grandlieu – this, remember it well, is not within the realm of dreams but firmly within that of reality; this aeroplane exists. Can you procure one for me tomorrow? And when it alights upon the water, the “Goëland” sits as gracefully as a yacht of fifty tons.

There are many misconceptions in public opinion regarding the lifespan of an aeroplane and a seaplane. A nine thousand dollar aeroplane, for example, will last three years and accomplish approximately 200,000 kilometers; one may therefore compare it very favorably to an automobile of similar price. The market life of a model such as the “J.N.” will extend over three seasons; many "Goeland" already in service have recorded thirty thousand kilometers upon their counters.

But is it necessary to examine an aeroplane after each flight? No; even without requiring the slightest visit. However, should a visit be necessary, your pilot will cost two hundred francs per week – and this sum will be accounted for in your final reckoning, alongside the Georgian wages of the pilot and mechanic, the oil, gasoline, repairs, garage fees, insurance, and a "Loriot" - all amounting to two francs per kilometer, and a “T.N.”

There are approximately forty thousand pilots’ licenses already distributed by the American and Italian authorities; the lack of pilots seems a very remote possibility even supposing that many of them do not desire to be professionals. If all things are thus – and they are - not only according to the authority of Vogue, but also according to the opinion of experts – why then does the public not fly?

My God! The reason is quite simple: the public does not fly because it believes flying is dangerous. 

But what of the automobile? One need only consider the percentage of air accidents compared with the percentage of automobile accidents - which, for example, occur at every circuit or somewhat important race. These remain in the hands of professionals who abuse them; alas, they provide occasion for painful lists of fatalities. Before the war, only those possessed by a devilish spirit would risk themselves in this youngest of human inventions; during the war, the energy of constructors was spent producing speed and mobility, while questions of comfort and safety were considered negligible factors. 

Since the war, since the peace – or at least what we call peace -

The desire for peace has developed a marvelous thing, a machine that soars and shines, no longer dull and tarnished.

Advance! A superior aeroplane, the “Aigle,” has been in development for approximately three years; it is currently capable of flight for seventy-five to one hundred hours, and you will have added approximately one hour’s transit time. Frenchwomen, Englishwomen—security well assured. 

As long as sport remains a pastime for someone, except perhaps for those who are accustomed to the skies, but since the war… (Continued from page 50) …the aeroplane is studied in every detail; each constitutive part has been examined with jealous care; woods have been selected that best suited certain purposes, and others which were most appropriate for other uses. Every curve has been calculated with mathematical precision. The weight of the mahogany propellers is measured to a hair’s breadth; each piece of steel must withstand five times the effort demanded of it—in short, everything is tested before being allowed to leave the factory. Each aeroplane is perfected. Everything is invented to make the air more accessible to those less fortunate and to tempt those less fortunate to take flight.

Thus, now, the aeroplane is an absolutely perfect object, and the chic woman has only one desire: to climb aboard. 

Let us now address a few practical suggestions: let the woman who does not seek novelty wait two years; I speak of the woman who dislikes horses, automobiles, and crossings—she would not be very comfortable attempting the experience of the air; but is it necessary to give her advice? Novelty holds no appeal for her; once she has never done something, she has no desire to do it. 

It must also be said to the woman who does not possess a great fortune that she should wait even longer, as aeroplanes are costly. For once she has tasted aerial piloting and found joy in it, it will be impossible for her to become an unhappy “pebble.”

As for all other women—the calves, the lilies of the valley, the new ones—let them note all novelties, both those of the mind and those of costume; for these, the air is the limitless field of the future. If you are under thirty-five years old, little Madame, have an aeroplane and a pilot, and you are still young enough to realize automatically at the critical moment what one has taught you in a lesson—be your own pilot.

A NEW SCHEDULE 

And if you are fortunate enough to be one of those rare women who know how to procure joys when destiny fails to provide them, what then? If you have an aeroplane of your own…

You will forget your adorers during the strolls you take before or after dinner, and surrender yourself to landscapes that seem to slip between the wings of a bird. You will abandon all your dear friends of the Ritz or Claridge when caught in the whirlwinds of air which will overturn you, full sail, and who knows if, having definitively renounced marrying one of your adorers, you will not decide to join some international aerial league and go to evangelize the dullards of central Africa from the height of an aeroplane!

VOGUE demands a minute attention to detail; and each week brings a new thrill. Many still love hats tied on with ribbons, but be tranquil – you will forget them in the midst of these events. You will feel yourself as if borne by an electrical storm, for one year, so that the market may be less inclined to like them.
