IN AUTOMOBILE FROM THE COAST
OF ARGENT TO THE CÔTE D'AZUR

Lourdes, the most famous pilgrimage in the world. From all points of the globe, countless crowds come each year to kneel before the grotto of Massabielle; miracles number there; a fervent faith bursts forth; processions and masses accumulate along the Gave de Pau and thousands of pilgrims, at night carrying torches, circle the hills that dominate the town like an endless serpent of light.

The renown of Luchon dates back to the Romans when they discovered there the first saline waters; it is now a charming little city situated in a very beautiful setting amidst the Dies tourmarquent mountains of Spain. It is also a most smart and gay resort; numerous festivities are organized there, even flower battles, and an opera season functions until the end of September.

From Luchon, the road leads to Foix; there is something particularly beautiful to see there: it is the grotto of Mas d'Azil which is one of the most astonishing curiosities of the Pyrenees – a natural tunnel in the rock, long five hundred meters. This grotto is found only twenty-five kilometers from Foix.

Foix abounds in legend and historical memories, although of all its relics, the château alone offers some interest. But Carcassonne and its walls call to us; it is found only a hundred kilometers northeast and easily reached in an afternoon. The road abandons the mountains; the scene changes; the earth becomes redder, the hills are lost in mist, and the silvery foliage of olive trees appears, proving that the sun's rays grow warmer.

One must arrive at Carcassonne by way of the river road to procure the sensation of seeing it appear in a quite prestigious setting; it is like a city of dreams rising before you.

One desires them with their turrets, their embrasures, all steeped in golden gauze; one might almost believe it too exquisite to be real...
CARDASSONNE

The old city teems with romantic legends and relics of bygone days; it still vibrates with the clatter of arms and terrible deeds. The double wall that surrounds it is adorned with fifty conical towers, and their restoration by Viollet le Duc was executed with remarkable care; these towers now serve as barracks for French soldiers who inject an element of life and turbulent gaiety into these memories of the past.

The new city, on the other hand, is frankly modern; commercial life is concentrated at Place Carnot. Our automobile traverses the dusty plain of Languedoc and launches upon the national road leading to Béziers.

Béziers is a very colourful and picturesque town, but women in the evenings wear veils of metal mesh or fine lace, framing the brow, the veil falling only on one side and encircling the face. 

At the theatre where we are solicited each evening, the women are all daringly low-necked, but it is upon the stage that we find the most elegance. The actresses of Paris have a justified reputation for dressing admirably—

the city has nevertheless lost much of its ancient character, having been overrun by numerous modern houses, cafes and shops. It still possesses its cathedral with its beautiful rose windows and its Gothic cloister which lends it a moving dignity. From the terrace of the cathedral, the view extends northward over the Cévennes mountains that cut themselves against the distance, deliciously overlooking the Mediterranean Sea which shimmers silently and blue as a dreamlike ocean.

The road winds through fields and gardens; the air is dry, clear, gay; the sky is like blue marble and the red hills are crowned with silver olive trees that etch their slender lines upon the horizon. The gardens become ever more brilliant and after one hundred kilometers, Nîmes is reached. 

There is not a city on the Mediterranean which is more Greco-Roman than Nîmes; nor one which produces a more harmonious effect by the way in which its monuments are grouped. It remains lively and animated, filled with modern cafes and wonderfully noble edifices of the Maison Carrée with its Corinthian columns, among the most harmonious, the temple of Diana and the famous amphitheatre—a city from another age.

The arenas upon which so much has been written are the most perfect of Roman ruins; the arches, the recesses, the grandstands that once held twenty-four thousand souls – partially restored now – have served as settings for bullfights, a pleasure of old ages, and for cinema, the pleasure of modern times.

The end of our journey brings us to Avignon, this ancient city steeped in melancholy, which has held one of the most important places in the history of the Catholic Church; the Papal Palace is surely the finest example of civil Gothic architecture throughout the world. We return then to Arles, celebrated today for the Greek beauty of its women, as it always was.

And now, Marseille! A prosperous city, buzzing with activity; it is warm despite the proximity of the sea. The masts and chimneys in the port obscure the sky; a sense of agitation fills the air, everyone comes and goes, everyone bustles about, everyone acts. 

Then comes the Riviera: this siren calls to us with her songs of indolence and her smiles of crystalline sunshine; it is the voice of Cannes, Monte-Carlo, Nice.

The summits, the peaks of the Pyrenees are far away; so too are those charming or cheerful little towns nestled in their shaded valleys. Yet the memory of their beauties and their charms remains permanent in the spirit and in the heart of those who have had the joy of visiting them on a blue and golden September day.

ELEGANT
(Continued from page 21)

Many women adopt this style, and many are setting the mode. Soon, as the sun becomes more ardent, we shall be obliged to dress in light, luminous fabrics. Courses and Son Polo are already attracting the affections of those who love wide open spaces, and just as before the war, the gatherings, though perhaps not quite so elegant, are nonetheless numerous and very lively.

Fortunately, the colours are softened, nuanced; and to the south, from Nîmes, we pass between sumptuous memories of the past. The streets are brilliant with the light reflecting from the shops, while the lines of proportions are pleasing – “the arenas” make of Nîmes a city of walls and exteriors that are almost entirely restored.

And just now we had a missive summoning us to Auteuil. I have also known what it was to do nothing but slip into one’s habit when the gaslights ignite and depart at random, on an adventure, encountering a friend at the corner of the Madeleine—in those days did one not meet a friend?—and welcoming him with “Good evening, my brave man. It was then that I did you the honour of magnificent dinners at every house in the city, tables laden with roses. Surely, Eusèbe interrupted, for surely Monsieur le Comte would not have been looking. I cared so little that after three years the inheritance of my poor aunt threatened ruin. But that is all, affirms Eusèbe. Well! continue, existence was then so Parisian; one found credit everywhere. A good pencil, a good signature on notes and one managed to get by. I have been able to fabricate charming gowns, Monsieur le Comte, but I would not wish to trouble you; yet in my head I have the idea that there must remain at the cash desk a few small invoices of Monsieur le Comte. THE ELEGANCE FOR SMALLER PURSES

The drawing on page 47 at left and top represents a delightful little dress for warmth with simple straight lines adorned with embroidery and pleats on the sides. The silk is beige China, and the belt as well as the straight band turned back forming the collar are in reversible beige satin. The waistcoat is composed of alternating rows of Valenciennes and organdi with very small stitched folds. The scarf admirably suits travelling dresses for it is exceedingly light.

“THREE WEEKS IN MOROCCO”

From sunset, the impression is unforgettable and fairy-like. Fez is above all a market and a University. The Souks—markets—are a bustling and animated city at the centre of the calm great city. One sees donations borne on mules in these bazaars whose characteristic is the gathering of a single category of merchandise within each Souk: copperware, pottery, objects of tinwork, fabrics. It is there that one observes the activity of industry in Fez. This division by category of merchandise has lasted for several hundreds of years and our shops seem to have copied it.

The difference that strikes one between this establishment and our own is that the native merchant does not, so to speak, fix his price, and any transaction, however slight, gives rise to a very amusing haggling which, in my opinion, doubles the pleasure of making a purchase – a sort of playful exchange between buyer and seller.

Leaving the Souks, we direct ourselves towards the university city. (Continued from page 35) Monsieur le Comte may say so. Are these engagements written on paper? —Monsieur le Comte is jesting. “Otherwise, Eusebe; I shall pay you on the first day.” One must be in a certain humour to see how life becomes expensive.

Eusebe, do you know what I paid just now for a pair of boots? – The Count may not know what one demands for shirts, and then the laundry bills! A scandal! A shame! When one thinks that there are foreigners, in New York or elsewhere, who imagine that existence in Paris is a lark. Let them come here and discover it is no lark! (The Parisian darkens definitively.) For you, it’s not what it was. – Nothing costs too much anymore.

We were walking in the forest of Bondy. A group of friends have departed. Some have not returned from the war; others have met their end; you and I alone remain amidst a crowd of people whose faces give us pain. It is as if I had an urge to go and plant my cabbages in the countryside. If that appeals to you, I shall take you into my service, and from time to time, when we are rich, we will enjoy smelling the air of the capital and recalling the good days of yesteryear.
